cards.front: Why does a gamete carry only one allele of each gene, even though a body cell carries two?
cards.back: A body cell has **two alleles** per gene, one from each parent, and each gamete receives only one. **Chance** decides which of the parent's two alleles enters a given gamete.
cards.hint: Think about where a body cell's two alleles come from.

cards.front: What phenotype ratio do two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt) produce with complete dominance?
cards.back: **3 tall : 1 short**. Three of the four grid combinations (TT, Tt, Tt) contain T, so only tt is short.
cards.hint: Write the gametes first, then fill a 2×2 grid.

cards.front: Why does a TtRr × TtRr cross give a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio?
cards.back: Each parent makes **four equally common gamete types** (TR, Tr, tR, tr), giving sixteen equally likely combinations, because the two genes lie on different chromosomes.
cards.hint: Count how many gamete types each parent makes.

cards.back: A **dominant allele** is one that shows its effect in a heterozygous individual, masking any recessive allele present.

cards.front: A student says codominance means the heterozygote is an intermediate form. What is wrong?
cards.back: **Codominance is not blending.** Both alleles are fully expressed, so the heterozygote shows both effects rather than an intermediate form.
cards.hint: Ask whether both alleles are visible in the phenotype.

cards.front: In a Tt × Tt cross, how many of 80 offspring are short?
cards.back: **20 short plants**. Only tt is short, which is $\frac{1}{4}$ of offspring, so $\frac{1}{4}\times80=20$.
cards.hint: Work out what fraction of the grid is short before you multiply.

cards.front: In a TtRr × TtRr cross, how many of 160 offspring are tall with white flowers?
cards.back: **30 plants**. Tall white-flowered plants (T_rr) make up $\frac{3}{16}$ of offspring, so $\frac{3}{16}\times160=30$.
cards.hint: Look up this phenotype's proportion in the dihybrid table.

cards.front: Why do genes on the same chromosome break the 9:3:3:1 ratio?
cards.back: Linked genes tend to be **inherited together**, so parental combinations dominate. Only occasional crossing over separates the alleles, giving more parental types than the ratio predicts.
cards.hint: Compare where the two genes sit with what the ratio requires.

cards.back: A **carrier** is a heterozygous individual who has one copy of a recessive allele and does not show the condition it causes.

cards.front: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more often seen in males?
cards.back: Males are XY, so a **single recessive allele** on their one X chromosome shows in their phenotype. Females need two copies to show the condition.
cards.hint: Compare how many X chromosomes each sex has.

cards.front: Why can a male not be a carrier of an X-linked recessive allele?
cards.back: If a male has the allele he has the condition, because he has only one X chromosome. A **carrier** must be a heterozygous female.
cards.hint: Count the X chromosomes a male has.

cards.front: Which pedigree clue points to a recessive allele?
cards.back: **Unaffected parents with an affected child** point to a recessive allele, because the parents must each carry one copy without showing the condition.
cards.hint: Think about who shows the phenotype and who does not.

cards.front: Which pedigree clue rules out an X-linked recessive allele?
cards.back: An **affected daughter with an unaffected father** rules it out, because she would need to receive the allele from her father's X chromosome.
cards.hint: Think about which parent passes an X chromosome to a daughter.

cards.front: How can the environment change a phenotype without changing the genotype?
cards.back: Conditions such as soil acidity, diet or sunlight alter how a characteristic develops. Hydrangeas with the same genotype make **blue** flowers in acidic soil and **pink** in alkaline soil.
cards.hint: Think of a plant whose flower colour depends on what it grows in.
